title: Practical GraphRAG: Making LLMs smarter with Knowledge Graphs — Michael, Jesus, and Stephen, Neo4j

summary: Stephen Chin frames the problem: LLMs lack enterprise knowledge, hallucinate, and can't explain answers. Vector similarity isn't relevance; standard RAG returns incomplete, hard-to-explain results. GraphRAG uses knowledge graphs—nodes, relationships, properties—for richer, contextual, explainable, and secure answers. He cites Microsoft Research (lower token costs), Gartner 2024 hype cycle, LinkedIn (28.6% faster resolution), and data.world (3x accuracy improvement). Michael Hunger details the GraphRAG pipeline in three phases. First, constructing a lexical graph from unstructured documents with chunks connected by structure, sequence, and similarity. Second, entity extraction using LLMs with a graph schema and instruction prompts, optionally connecting to existing structured knowledge graphs such as CRM data enriched with call transcripts. Third, graph enrichment with algorithms like PageRank, clustering, and community summarization that identifies cross-document topic clusters. The search/retrieval phase goes beyond simple vector lookup: it performs an initial index search (vector, full-text, spatial, or hybrid) to find entry points, then follows relationships to fetch additional context. External user context—such as department affiliation—shapes which information is retrieved. Rather than returning text fragments, it returns a contextual subgraph to the LLM, and modern LLMs are increasingly trained on graph processing patterns. Michael demonstrates an open-source knowledge graph builder tool that processes PDFs, YouTube transcripts, Wikipedia articles, and web pages, extracting entities following a user-defined schema. A Google DeepMind example shows the connected lexical graph and entity graph with multiple retriever types and explainability views showing which sources, chunks, and entities were used. He also shows an agentic approach where domain-specific retrievers run individual Cypher queries in a loop, breaking user questions into tasks with parameter extraction. A GraphRAG Python package encapsulates construction and retrieval. Resources and patterns are available at graph.com.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: GraphRAG addresses LLM weaknesses—hallucinations, lack of domain knowledge, poor explainability—by grounding responses in structured knowledge graphs.

The construction pipeline has three phases: lexical graph building, LLM-based entity extraction (optionally connecting to existing KGs like CRM data), and graph enrichment with algorithms like PageRank and community summarization.
GraphRAG retrieval uses initial index searches to find entry points, then traverses relationships to return contextual subgraphs—not just text fragments—to LLMs.
External user context (e.g., department, role) shapes retrieval, enabling role-based access and personalized responses.
Community summarization identifies cross-document topic clusters, revealing recurring themes across many documents.
Modern LLMs are increasingly trained on graph processing, enabling them to handle node-relationship-node patterns as context.
An open-source knowledge graph builder tool extracts entities from PDFs, YouTube transcripts, Wikipedia, and web articles following user-defined schemas.
Agentic GraphRAG uses domain-specific retrievers running individual Cypher queries, breaking questions into tasks with parameter extraction.
GraphRAG provides explainability by showing which sources, chunks, and entities contributed to each answer.
Understand why GraphRAG improves over standard vector-based RAG in relevance, context, and explainability

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Backgrounds
sections.summary: Michael Hunger and Stephen Chin introduce themselves as Neo4j leaders co-authoring 'GraphRAG: The Definitive Guide' for O'Reilly. Stephen previews the structure: he covers high-level GraphRAG concepts, Michael dives into patterns and details.

sections.title: The Case for GraphRAG
sections.summary: Stephen argues LLMs lack enterprise knowledge, hallucinate, and can't explain answers. Vector RAG is incomplete—vector similarity isn't relevance. Knowledge graphs (nodes, relationships, properties) provide richer context, explainability, and security. Cites Microsoft GraphRAG paper (lower token costs), Gartner 2024 hype cycle, LinkedIn (28.6% faster resolution), and data.world (3x accuracy improvement).

sections.title: GraphRAG Construction Pipeline and Patterns
sections.summary: Michael details GraphRAG construction: (1) build lexical graph from documents with chunks connected by structure, sequence, and similarity; (2) entity extraction using LLMs with graph schema, instruction prompts, and optionally existing ground truth; (3) graph enrichment with algorithms like PageRank and community summarization. References patterns catalog at graph.com with named patterns, descriptions, contexts, and queries.

sections.title: Graph Enrichment and Search/Retrieval Phase
sections.summary: Michael continues construction: connecting extracted entities to existing knowledge graphs (e.g., CRM enriched with call transcripts), graph algorithm enrichment (clustering, community summarization identifying cross-document topic clusters). He then covers the search phase: initial index search (vector, full-text, spatial, hybrid) to find entry points, followed by relationship traversal to fetch additional context. External user context (e.g., department) shapes retrieval. Returns a contextual subgraph—not just text fragments—to the LLM, noting modern LLMs are increasingly trained on graph processing patterns.

sections.title: Demos: Knowledge Graph Builder and Agentic Retrieval
sections.summary: Michael demos an open-source knowledge graph builder tool processing PDFs, YouTube transcripts, Wikipedia articles, and web pages. A Google DeepMind example shows the lexical graph (documents + chunks) and entity graph (companies, locations, people, technologies) following a user-defined schema. Multiple retriever types (vector, graph+full-text, entity) are available with explainability views showing which sources, chunks, and entities were used, plus RAGAS evaluation. He shows an agentic approach with domain-specific retrievers running individual Cypher queries in a tool-calling loop, and a GraphRAG Python package encapsulating construction and retrieval with Neo4j integration and notebook visualization.

sections.title: Closing and Resources
sections.summary: Michael points to graph.com for all resources, patterns, and community contributions. Stephen closes by thanking attendees and inviting questions at the Neo4j booth.
